item.title: Lynch syndrome
item.description:
Lynch syndrome is the most common inherited cancer predisposition syndrome, affecting approximately one in 350-450 individuals, yet the majority of carriers remain undiagnosed, representing a substantial and preventable public health burden. Caused by germline pathogenic variants in DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes, Lynch syndrome confers markedly elevated and heterogeneous risks of colorectal, endometrial, and multiple extracolonic cancers. Advances in molecular diagnostics, particularly universal tumour testing for MMR deficiency, have transformed case identification and enabled targeted germline testing and cascade screening of relatives at risk. Despite these advances, implementation remains inconsistent, with substantial attrition across diagnostic pathways and inequities in access to care. Preventive strategies-including colonoscopic surveillance, aspirin chemoprevention, and risk-reducing surgery-are effective but require gene-specific and individualised application. Therapeutically, the immunogenic biology of MMR-deficient tumours has positioned Lynch syndrome at the forefront of precision oncology, with immune checkpoint inhibitors delivering substantial benefit and emerging vaccine strategies offering promise for cancer interception. In this Review, we provide an integrated overview of Lynch syndrome across the continuum of care, highlighting advances in biology, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment, while emphasising the crucial need to align scientific progress with equitable and effective health-system delivery.

item.title: Empirical tuberculosis treatment in infants living with HIV hospitalised with severe pneumonia in Africa (EMPIRICAL): a multicentre, randomised, open-label, 2 × 2 factorial, controlled superiority trial
item.description:
Background: Mortality among infants with severe HIV-associated pneumonia remains high globally. The EMPIRICAL trial evaluated whether empirical tuberculosis treatment (eTB-T) improves survival compared with the currently recommended microbiologically and clinically guided strategy.

Methods: This multicentre, open-label, group-sequential designed, 2×2 factorial, randomised, controlled, superiority trial was conducted in 19 hospitals across Côte d'Ivoire, Malawi, Mozambique, Uganda, Zambia, and Zimbabwe. Infants aged 28-365 days admitted with severe HIV-associated pneumonia, without a current tuberculosis diagnosis or contact, were centrally and individually randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) using a secure web-based system stratified by site and severity. A computer-generated block randomisation schedule was used, with fixed blocks of eight allocations (two allocations to each factorial treatment group) within each stratum. Participants received standard of care (SoC) comprising treatment for bacterial (WHO-recommended antibiotics) and Pneumocystis jirovecii (cotrimoxazole and steroids) pneumonia, SoC plus 15 days of oral valganciclovir (16 mg/kg per 12 h), or SoC plus 6 months of tuberculosis treatment (isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 2 months, plus isoniazid and rifampicin for 4 subsequent months), or both interventions combined. Here, we report the comparison between the eTB-T (ie, SoC plus tuberculosis treatment and SoC plus oral valganciclovir plus tuberculosis treatment) and non-eTB-T (ie, SoC or SoC plus 15 days of oral valganciclovir) groups. Nasopharyngeal aspirates, stools for Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra testing, and urine for tuberculosis lipoarabinomannan assay were collected at recruitment. In the non-eTB-T groups, tuberculosis treatment was initiated if microbiological results collected at recruitment yielded positive results or if, during follow-up, the treating clinician suspected tuberculosis on clinical grounds, including radiological findings, in accordance with routine clinical practice and guidelines. The primary endpoint was all-cause mortality (at 15 days and 360 days). Survival was estimated using flexible parametric models with covariate-adjusted conditional estimates; missing data were imputed by chained equations. The trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03915366) and is now complete.

Findings: Between March 15, 2020, and Jan 31, 2024, 563 participants were enrolled; 558 were analysed after excluding five patients who did not meet eligibility criteria. 276 participants were allocated to the eTB-T groups (n=140 eTB-T and n=136 valganciclovir plus eTB-T) and 282 to the non-eTB-T groups (n=142 SoC and n=140 valganciclovir). 17 (6%) of 276 in the eTB-T groups and 20 (7%) of 282 in the non-eTB-T groups were lost to follow-up. Median age was 4·4 months (IQR 3·2-7·4) and 274 (49%) of participants were female and 284 (51%) were male. In the non-eTB-T groups, 130 (46%) of 282 participants eventually initiated tuberculosis treatment at a median of 4·0 days (IQR 3·0-15·0) after recruitment due to positive microbiological findings in 55 (20%) cases (53 confirmed by tuberculosis lipoarabinomannan assay and two by nasopharyngeal aspirates Xpert MTB/RIF) or clinical decision in 75 (27%) cases. There was no evidence of interaction between valganciclovir and eTB-T (adjusted hazard ratio 1·19, 95% CI 0·73-1·95; pheterogeneity=0·4836). At 12 months, 132 (48%) of 276 participants in eTB-T groups and 121 (43%) of 282 participants in non-eTB-T groups died. In the eTB-T groups, the adjusted hazard ratio for death was 1·12 (95% CI 0·87-1·43; p=0·3868). At 15 days, the odds ratio was 1·24 (95% CI 0·83-1·84; p=0·2950). Serious adverse events did not differ between groups (1·19, 0·82-1·73; p=0·3523). There were no treatment-related deaths. The most common adverse events were elevation of transaminases (72 [26%] cases in the eTB-T groups and 74 [26%] in the non-eTB-T group), anaemia (163 [59%] cases in the eTB-T groups and 169 [60%] in the non-eTB-T groups), and infectious disease requiring antimicrobial treatment (161 [58%] cases in the eTB-T groups and 176 [62%] in the non-eTB-T groups).

Interpretation: In contrast to empirical treatment with valganciclovir, there was no evidence that eTB-T was superior to a clinically and microbiologically guided strategy in reducing all-cause mortality among infants with HIV-associated pneumonia. However, the high proportion of infants who eventually initiated tuberculosis treatment during follow-up in the non-eTB-T groups might have reduced the contrast between strategies and attenuated the ability to detect differences in outcomes.

item.title: Trevogrumab (anti-GDF8) with or without garetosmab (anti-activin A) for prevention of muscle loss during semaglutide-induced weight reduction in people with obesity (COURAGE): a two-part, phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial
item.description:
Background: Rapid weight loss, as induced by GLP-1 receptor agonists, is accompanied by pronounced muscle loss. GDF8 (myostatin) and activin A (ActA), acting via ActRIIA/B receptors, are negative regulators of muscle mass. The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of antibodies blocking GDF8 (trevogrumab) and ActA (garetosmab) on semaglutide-induced weight and muscle loss.

Methods: COURAGE is a two-part, phase 2, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised trial. This multicentre (60 sites), US-based trial enrolled participants aged 18-80 years with obesity (BMI ≥30 kg/m2). In part A, participants were treated for 26 weeks with semaglutide (titrated to 2·4 mg subcutaneously weekly) in addition to a randomly assigned (1:1:1:1) concomitant treatment: placebo, trevogrumab 200 mg, trevogrumab 400 mg, or trevogrumab 400 mg and garetosmab 10 mg/kg. Trevogrumab was administered subcutaneously weekly and garetosmab was administered intravenously every 4 weeks. Part A also included a subsequent semaglutide withdrawal period, at which point participants (randomly assigned at baseline 1:1 within each group) received either trevogrumab 400 mg or placebo for an additional 26 weeks. In part B, participants were treated with semaglutide for 52 weeks and randomly assigned (1:2:2) to concomitant treatment with placebo, trevogrumab 25 mg, or trevogrumab 75 mg. Groups were stratified according to sex, BMI (<35 kg/m2vs ≥35 kg/m2), and participation in an exploratory MRI substudy assessing thigh muscle volume. Study participants, the principal investigators, and study site personnel were masked to all randomisation assignments throughout the study. Primary endpoints were percent change in lean mass, fat mass, and bodyweight from baseline to week 26 (part A) or week 52 (part B). Efficacy and safety analyses were done in all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of a study drug (efficacy, as randomly assigned; safety, as treated). COURAGE is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06299098, and is currently active, not recruiting.

Findings: 975 participants were enrolled between June 21, 2024, and April 14, 2025. Mean age was 49·0 years (SD 13·2) and mean BMI was 36·7 kg/m2 (SD 5·0); 627 (64%) of 975 participants were female and 348 (36%) were male. In part A (n=605, of whom n=599 received at least one dose of study drug), a substantial decrease in lean mass was observed in the semaglutide plus placebo group at week 26 (-6·6% [95% CI -7·4 to -5·7]); the estimated treatment difference (ETD) versus semaglutide plus placebo was +3·1% (95% CI 1·9 to 4·3) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 200 mg, +2·7% (1·5 to 4·0) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg, and +4·5% (3·1 to 5·9) with semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg. In part B (n=376), lean mass percent change from baseline to week 52 for semaglutide plus placebo was -7·3% (-8·8 to -5·8); the ETD versus semaglutide plus placebo was +1·5% (-0·3 to 3·3) for semaglutide plus trevogrumab 25 mg, and +3·1% (1·3 to 4·9) for semaglutide plus trevogrumab 75 mg. Change from baseline in fat mass in part A was -15·6% (-17·4 to -13·9) in the semaglutide plus placebo group; the ETD was significant in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg group (-3·4% [-5·9 to -0·9]) and the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (-11·7% [-14·4 to -9·0]) in part A. No other groups in part A nor any in part B had significantly different changes in fat mass compared with semaglutide plus placebo. Percent change in bodyweight in part A was -10·6 (-11·6 to -9·7) in the semaglutide plus placebo group; the ETD was significant for the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (-2·7 [-4·1 to -1·2]). No other groups in part A nor any in part B had significantly different changes in bodyweight compared with semaglutide plus placebo. Semaglutide plus trevogrumab (25 mg, 75 mg, 200 mg, or 400 mg) was generally well tolerated with a safety profile similar to semaglutide plus placebo; however, semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg had a high incidence of serious adverse events (14 [9%] of 149) and treatment discontinuations (48 [32%] of 149). Gastrointestinal adverse events were the most commonly reported, and they occurred with similar incidence across treatment groups. Muscle spasms occurred more frequently in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group (61 [41%] of 149) compared with the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 200 mg or 400 mg groups (23 [8%] of 299) and semaglutide plus placebo groups (seven [5%] of 151). Most adverse events were mild to moderate in severity. Two deaths occurred during the study, both in the semaglutide plus trevogrumab 400 mg plus garetosmab 10 mg/kg group; a causal association between treatment and these events was not identified.

Interpretation: This study establishes proof of concept for GDF8 inhibition by trevogrumab alone as a generally well tolerated strategy to preserve lean mass during GLP-1 receptor agonist-induced weight loss. Although the addition of ActA inhibition by garetosmab further improved body composition and weight loss, the combination did not have favourable safety and tolerability. Further study is required to understand whether improved body composition during weight loss might preserve physical function and overall metabolic health.

item.title: A blended digital parenting intervention for the prevention of sexual violence, exploitative sex, and maltreatment of children at scale in Tanzania: a cluster-randomised, controlled trial
item.description:
Background: Childhood sexual, physical, and verbal violence are global public health priorities, affecting 1 billion children each year. ParentApp integrates sexual violence prevention into WHO-UNICEF's open-access Parenting for Lifelong Health programme, using innovative blended digital delivery. We aimed to test the efficacy of ParentApp in preventing sexual violence and maltreatment against adolescent-aged children and improving preventive mechanisms such as family mental health and adolescent-caregiver relationships.

Methods: This cluster-randomised, controlled trial was conducted in 80 Tanzanian sub-wards. Participants were primary caregivers aged 18 years and older and their adolescents (aged 10-17 years). Sub-wards were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either ParentApp (intervention group) or a control WASHApp programme. Clusters were randomly assigned in blocks of six, stratified by urban versus rural location. Statisticians carrying out randomisation and data analysts were masked; it was not possible to mask participants or researchers. Intervention groups received a low-cost Android phone installed with ParentApp, a 12-module offline-first app, with one in-person orientation session and remote support via WhatsApp group chats, at a delivery cost of US$6 per family at scale, or $10 with 20% smartphone provision. Control groups received a low-cost Android phone installed with WASHApp, a 12-module offline-first app for water, sanitation, and hygiene, with one in-person orientation session. The primary outcomes were adolescent sexual violence victimisation and maltreatment and high-risk situations for sexual violence, assessed in all participants irrespective of uptake and engagement at 5 months and 18 months post-baseline. The trial was registered on March 14, 2023, with OSF (https://osf.io/t9fxz) and is completed.

Findings: Between May 11 and Oct 9, 2023, 2692 caregiver-adolescent dyads were screened for study eligibility; 2396 adolescents (1217 [50·8%] female and 1179 [49·2%] male) and 2396 caregivers (1795 [74·9%] female and 601 [25·1%] male) were recruited. 2145 (89·5%) adolescents and 2252 (94·0%) caregivers were retained in the study and included in analyses at 18 months. Adolescent girls in ParentApp clusters had a substantial reduction in past-month sexual violence victimisation compared with those in control clusters (incidence rate ratio [IRR] 0·43 [95% CI 0·21-0·86]; p=0·018), with no effect for boys (1·21 [0·59-2·43]; p=0·60). Past-month maltreatment (physical abuse, verbal abuse, and neglect) was lower in ParentApp clusters than in control clusters (adolescent report IRR 0·92 [0·88-0·96]; p<0·0001, caregiver report 0·87 [0·82-0·92]; p<0·0001). Past-month exposure to high-risk situations for sexual violence was lower in ParentApp clusters than in control clusters (adolescent girls IRR 0·87 [0·77-0·97]; p=0·012, adolescent boys 0·85 [0·79-0·91]; p<0·0001, caregiver report 0·81 [0·75-0·88]; p<0·0001). There were no reported adverse events.

Interpretation: A low-cost blended digital parenting programme in countries such as Tanzania could simultaneously reduce childhood sexual violence (for girls) and maltreatment and sexual violence risk situations (for girls and boys).

item.title: Reframing disease elimination: an update from the Lancet Commission on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
item.description:
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, with increasing global burden driven by population growth and ageing, persistent harmful exposures, and substantial health inequities. The Lancet Commission on COPD articulated an ambitious vision for disease elimination with prevention, early detection, and intervention. This Review revisits that vision, assesses progress since 2022, and calls for a broader commitment to lifelong lung health as an update of the Commission. Across seven sections, this Review advances a unified framework integrating the biology of lung development and ageing, precision medicine, patient-centred outcomes, and regulatory reform. COPD is not a single, uniform disease; rather, a biologically complex condition shaped by genetic, developmental, environmental, infectious, and behavioural factors across the entire life course. Effective prevention and care should therefore move beyond the detection and treatment of late physiological impairment toward earlier disease recognition, biological stratification, and interventions to preserve lung health, reduce symptoms, and prevent morbidity and premature mortality. The Review charts a path from reactive, late-stage management toward proactive, equitable, precision-based prevention and care. The central premise is unequivocal: the global burden of COPD can be substantially reduced. Success should be measured not only by gains in lung function and survival but also by improvements in daily functioning, quality of life, and wellbeing. In this expanded vision, COPD is no longer viewed solely as a chronic disease to be managed but as a preventable and modifiable condition within a broader commitment to lifelong lung health.

item.title: Cardiovascular outcomes with survodutide in adults with obesity at increased cardiovascular risk (SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT): a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial
item.description:
Background: Survodutide, a glucagon receptor and GLP-1 receptor dual agonist, improved markers of cardiometabolic health in people with obesity, but cardiovascular safety for this new class remains to be established.

Methods: SYNCHRONIZE-CVOT was a global, phase 3, randomised, double-blind, parallel-group, placebo-controlled, multicentre, event-driven, cardiovascular safety trial conducted at 524 clinical sites in 34 countries. We included participants aged 18 years or older with a BMI of 27 kg/m2 or greater and established cardiovascular disease or at least two obesity complications or risk factors for cardiovascular disease; participants with chronic kidney disease were eligible if they also had a BMI of 30 kg/m2 or greater. Participants were randomly assigned by interactive response technology (1:1:1) to once-weekly subcutaneous survodutide (up-titrated to 3·6 mg or 6·0 mg) or placebo. The primary endpoint was a composite of death from cardiovascular causes, non-fatal stroke, non-fatal myocardial infarction, ischaemia-related coronary revascularisation, or heart failure event (targeting 189 primary endpoint events). We assessed the non-inferiority of pooled survodutide compared with placebo with a margin of 1·65 for the upper limit of the two-sided 95% CI of the hazard ratio (HR). Efficacy and safety analyses included all randomly assigned participants who received at least one dose of survodutide or placebo. The primary analysis was performed according to the treatment-regimen estimand, which assessed treatment effects regardless of any early discontinuation of survodutide or placebo, temporary stop, the use of protocol-prohibited obesity medications, or a prolonged dose-escalation period. This completed trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06077864.

Findings: From Nov 20, 2023, to Nov 8, 2024, we screened 7753 participants, of whom 5530 (71·3%) participants were recruited and randomly assigned to treatment. 23 (0·4%) participants were not treated; 1836 (33·3%) of 5507 participants received survodutide 3·6 mg, 1835 (33·3%) received 6·0 mg, and 1836 (33·3%) received placebo; 2194 (39·8%) were female, 3313 (60·2%) were male, and 4332 (78·7%) were White. Median time in study was 22·0 months (IQR 20·1-23·7). 1029 (56·0%) in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, 1039 (56·6%) in the survodutide 6·0 mg group, and 1083 (59·0%) in the placebo group remained on treatment until study closeout. The primary endpoint occurred in 136 (3·7%) of 3671 participants in the survodutide group and in 76 (4·1%) 1836 participants in the placebo group (HR 0·89 [95% CI 0·67-1·18; p<0·0001 for non-inferiority). Adverse events occurred in 1708 (93·0%) of 1836 participants with survodutide 3·6 mg, 1708 (93·1%) of 1835 with survodutide 6·0 mg, and 1571 (85·6%) of 1836 with placebo. Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent with survodutide than in the placebo group (nausea occurred in 882 [48·0%] of 1836 participants in the 3·6 mg group and 900 [49·0%] of 1835 in the 6·0 mg group vs 223 [12·1%] of 1836 in the placebo group, and vomiting occurred in 582 [31·7%] participants in the 3·6 mg group and 623 [34·0%] in the 6·0 mg group vs 89 [4·8%] in the placebo group). Gastrointestinal adverse events leading to treatment discontinuations occurred in 354 (19·3%) participants in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, 381 (20·8%) in the survodutide 6·0 mg, and 34 (1·9%) in the placebo group. Serious adverse events occurred at similar rates across treatment groups (413 [22·5%] in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, 381 [20·8%] in the survodutide 6·0 mg, and 439 [23·9%] in the placebo group). Fatal adverse events were similar across treatment groups (16 [0·9%] in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, 16 [0·9%] in the survodutide 6·0 mg, and 11 [0·6%] in the placebo group) and were primarily due to cardiac disorders (six [0·3%] in the survodutide 3·6 mg group, seven [0·4%] in the survodutide 6·0 mg, and six [0·3%] in the placebo group).

Interpretation: In participants with obesity with established cardiovascular disease or chronic kidney disease or at increased risk of cardiovascular disease, survodutide was not associated with increased risk for the primary composite endpoint of death from cardiovascular causes, non-fatal stroke, non-fatal myocardial infarction, ischaemia-related coronary revascularisation, or heart failure event compared with placebo. This cardiovascular safety trial provides clinicians with reassuring data that treatment with survodutide, a novel glucagon receptor-GLP-1 receptor dual agonist, is not associated with increased cardiovascular risk.

item.title: Efficacy and safety of efinopegdutide in adults with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis and stage 2-3 fibrosis: a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled study
item.description:
Background: Efinopegdutide is a pharmacologically distinct once-weekly GLP-1-glucagon receptor co-agonist with a relative receptor potency balance of approximately 2:1 under development for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH). We aimed to investigate the efficacy and safety of efinopegdutide in adults with non-cirrhotic MASH.

Methods: We did a phase 2b, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind study conducted at 176 academic and community centres in 26 countries. We included adults (aged ≥18 years) with biopsy-confirmed MASH and stage 2 or stage 3 fibrosis. Eligible participants were randomly assigned (1:1:1:1:1) to receive either efinopegdutide (4 mg, 7 mg, or 10 mg), placebo, or open-label semaglutide 2·4 mg, all administered subcutaneously once weekly. Randomisation was performed centrally. The primary endpoint was MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis at week 52. The key secondary histological endpoint was fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis. Missing end-of-treatment biopsies were considered as failure for the primary analysis. This study is registered with EU CT, 2022-502647-35-00, and ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05877547, and is complete.

Findings: Between June 23, 2023, and Dec 29, 2025, we screened 1704 participants. We randomly assigned 386 (23%) participants, of whom 381 (99%; 194 [51%] women and 187 [49%] men) received at least one dose of study intervention and were included in the analysis. Baseline characteristics were similar across groups; 239 (63%) of 381 participants had F2 fibrosis and 142 (37%) had F3 fibrosis; the mean age of participants was 53 years (SD 13). At week 52, MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis occurred in 31 (56%) of 55 participants in the 4 mg efinopegdutide group, 31 (63%) of 49 participants in the 7 mg efinopegdutide group, and 35 (61%) of 57 participants in the 10 mg efinopegdutide group versus seven (13%) of 53 participants in the placebo group (difference vs placebo 43·0 percentage points [95% CI 25·7 to 57·8; p<0·0001] for 4 mg, 49·5 percentage points [31·4 to 64·2; p<0·0001] for 7 mg, and 47·8 percentage points [30·7 to 62·0; p<0·0001] for 10 mg); 26 (53%) of 49 participants receiving semaglutide met this endpoint. For the key secondary endpoint, fibrosis improvement of at least one stage without worsening of steatohepatitis occurred in 32 (43%) of 75 participants in the efinopegdutide 4 mg group, 39 (52%) of 75 participants in the 7 mg efinopegdutide group, and 26 (34%) of 77 participants in the efinopegdutide 10 mg group versus 16 (21%) of 77 participants receiving placebo (difference vs placebo 21·7 percentage points [7·1 to 35·7; p=0·0038] in the efinopegdutide 4 mg group, 30·4 percentage points [15·4 to 44·3; p<0·0001] in the efinopegdutide 7 mg group, and 13·0 percentage points [-1·2 to 26·8; p=0·072] in the efinopegdutide 10 mg group); 16 (25%) of 65 participants receiving semaglutide met this endpoint. The most frequently reported adverse events with efinopegdutide were gastrointestinal, with the highest rates among participants receiving efinopegdutide 10 mg. Adverse events leading to discontinuation of study intervention occurred more frequently among participants receiving efinopegdutide 10 mg (nine [11%] of 79 participants) compared with the other doses of efinopegdutide (range 3-4%) or placebo (one [1%]).

Interpretation: Treatment with efinopegdutide resulted in a significantly greater proportion of participants with MASH resolution without worsening of fibrosis compared with placebo. The 7 mg dose showed the most favourable benefit-risk profile, improving fibrosis by at least one stage without worsening steatohepatitis in approximately half of participants after 1 year of treatment. These findings support the potential utility of efinopegdutide as a once-weekly GLP-1-glucagon receptor co-agonist in MASH.

item.title: Cangrelor versus crushed ticagrelor in acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (DAPT-SHOCK-AMI): a randomised, double-blind trial
item.description:
Background: Acute myocardial infarction complicated by cardiogenic shock (AMI-CS) can compromise the administration and absorption of oral P2Y12 inhibitors and carries high ischaemic and mortality risks. This trial assessed whether intravenous cangrelor was non-inferior to crushed oral ticagrelor for short-term clinical outcomes and whether it provided faster and more consistent platelet inhibition in patients with AMI-CS.

Methods: DAPT-SHOCK-AMI was a double-blind trial conducted at 29 hospitals across five European countries (Czech Republic, France, Germany, Poland, and Slovakia). Patients older than 18 years with AMI-CS were randomly assigned (1:1 ratio, stratified by centre, age, sex, presence or absence of ST-segment elevation, and mechanical ventilation) to cangrelor (30 μg/kg bolus followed by an infusion of 4 μg/kg per min for at least 2 h) or crushed ticagrelor (180 mg loading dose). The primary laboratory endpoint was a platelet reactivity index of less than 50% at the end of primary percutaneous coronary intervention. The primary clinical endpoint was death, myocardial infarction, or ischaemic stroke at 30 days. The primary clinical endpoint was analysed for non-inferiority with a prespecified margin of 1 percentage point among all randomly assigned patients who received study treatment. The study is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT03551964) and EudraCT (2018-002161-19); recruitment and 1-year follow-up are complete, and 5-year follow-up is ongoing.

Findings: Between Aug 1, 2018, and Jan 19, 2024, 605 patients (137 [23%] were female) were randomly assigned to cangrelor (n=298) or ticagrelor (n=307); no surviving patients were lost to the 1-year follow-up. The primary laboratory endpoint was analysed in 56 (19%) patients in the cangrelor group and 68 (22%) in the ticagrelor group, and was achieved in 56 (100%) of 56 patients receiving cangrelor and 15 (22%) of 68 receiving ticagrelor (p<0·0001). The 30-day primary clinical endpoint occurred in 112 (38%) of 298 patients receiving cangrelor and 126 (41%) of 307 receiving ticagrelor; non-inferiority was not demonstrated (difference -4 percentage points [90% CI -10 to 3]; Pnon-inferiority=0·13). Major bleeding at 30 days occurred in 19 (6%) of 298 patients receiving cangrelor and 16 (5%) of 307 receiving ticagrelor.

Interpretation: To our knowledge, this is the first randomised trial to compare P2Y12 inhibitor strategies specifically in patients with AMI-CS. Cangrelor achieved effective platelet inhibition more frequently than crushed ticagrelor at the end of primary percutaneous coronary intervention. Non-inferiority of cangrelor versus crushed ticagrelor was not demonstrated for the primary 30-day clinical endpoint. These trial findings can inform future trials of P2Y12 inhibition strategies in patients with AMI-CS.
